findings.evidence: You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review.
findings.fix: Pick one term for the thing being tracked through intake, reconciliation, and payout, and use it consistently in this section and everywhere else in the document; if "stipend item" names something genuinely distinct from "the request," define that distinction explicitly.
findings.violation: The term "the stipend item" is introduced here and used three times, but it never appears anywhere else in the document, which otherwise refers to the same subject matter as "the stipend," "the request," and "reimbursement." A section titled Terminology Notes is where a reader would expect these terms reconciled, but instead a fourth, undefined term is added, so the reader cannot tell whether "the stipend item" names the equipment purchased, the reimbursement claim, or the portal request.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.fix: State the governing rule first, e.g. "The stipend applies only when all three of the following are true," then list the three conditions underneath it as a list.
findings.violation: Three consecutive sentences each read as a standalone sufficient condition ("if X, the stipend can apply"), and only the fourth sentence reveals that all three are jointly required. A reader who stops after any one of the first three sentences, which is plausible since each reads as a complete rule, would wrongly conclude that satisfying it alone is enough; the governing AND-rule arrives only after the exceptions/conditions that it actually governs.

findings.evidence: Approval Timeline: "The request is reviewed within two business days. The manager confirms the equipment category matches the approved list." Required Documentation: "The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion..." Review Responsibility: "The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out." Program Coordination: "The benefits team coordinates every stipend request from intake to payout... routes the request to the correct approver based on department."
findings.fix: Consolidate the approval chain into one section that states, in order, every reviewer a request passes through and the condition that triggers each (manager, then finance office for amounts over $200, then benefits-team scheduling), and remove the restatement from the other sections.
findings.location: Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Review Responsibility, and Program Coordination sections
findings.violation: The document never states the approval process as one sequence; instead each of four non-adjacent sections states a different, partial piece of it (a 2-day manager review, a separate finance-office review for requests over $200, and a benefits-team routing step), with no section cross-referencing the others or stating the order in which they occur relative to each other. A reader trying to answer "who approves my request and in what order" has to assemble the answer from four scattered sections rather than reading it once in the sequence it actually happens.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter. A copy of each update goes to the shared benefits folder the same day. Similarly, the IT asset group tracks the stipend budget each quarter. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time.
findings.fix: Replace or precede this section with a sentence or two stating what the stipend is and who it is for, and move the log-publishing and budget-tracking logistics to a section about recordkeeping.
findings.violation: A reader who reads only the section's first and last sentences ("The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter" / "Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time") cannot state what a section titled Program Overview is about; nothing in the section explains what the stipend program actually is, who it is for, or what it covers. The section instead moves through three loosely related administrative sub-topics (log publishing, budget tracking, copy requests) with no throughline connecting them to an overview of the program.

findings.evidence: The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter. A copy of each update goes to the shared benefits folder the same day. Similarly, the IT asset group tracks the stipend budget each quarter. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time.
findings.fix: Keep one running subject across the passage (for example, the benefits team) and route the other actors through it, or split the budget-tracking sentence into its own clearly introduced topic.
findings.violation: Across these four sentences the grammatical subject changes almost every time (the people operations office, a copy, the IT asset group, staff) with no sentence's subject picking up the topic the previous sentence just established; "Similarly" signals a parallel rather than a continuation, so the reader has to re-orient at nearly every sentence boundary.

findings.evidence: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: End the sentence on the critical new fact, e.g. "...because the manager is traveling and nobody told the backup reviewer that the request still needs sign-off."
findings.violation: The sentence's newest and most important information is that the backup reviewer was never told the request needs sign-off, but that lands in the middle of the sentence; the final position is occupied instead by "before the portal releases the confirmation email," an already-implied procedural detail, so the reader's attention lands on the least important part of the sentence rather than the actual blocking problem.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: The benefits team coordinates every stipend request from intake to payout. The team logs each request the moment it arrives. The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department.
findings.fix: Either cut this section or retitle and mark it explicitly as internal process documentation separate from the employee-facing policy, so the employee reader can tell it is not theirs to act on.
findings.violation: The section describes the benefits team's own internal routing workflow rather than anything the document's addressed reader (the employee applying for the stipend) needs to know or act on, and nothing signals that this content is for a different, internal audience; the rest of the document otherwise speaks directly to the applying employee (e.g. "Employees start a stipend request," "You must keep your equipment in good working condition").

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.
